title: .NET Backend Interview Track
description: 24-topic senior .NET backend interview preparation with answers, practical examples and working C# examples.

questions.question: What is the difference between a value type and a reference type in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Value types contain their value directly, while reference-type variables hold a reference to an object. Assigning a value type copies the value; assigning a reference type copies the reference.
questions.detailedAnswer: Value types contain their value directly, while reference-type variables hold a reference to an object. Assigning a value type copies the value; assigning a reference type copies the reference.
questions.example: An ATM transaction amount is a decimal value, while an ATM service object is a reference-type object shared through its reference.
questions.seniorPerspective: At senior level, connect this to mutation, boxing, allocations and API design rather than stopping at stack-versus-heap wording.
questions.memoryCue: Value = copy the value; reference = copy the reference.

questions.question: What is the difference between var, object and dynamic?
questions.shortAnswer: var is compile-time type inference; object is the base type and may require casting; dynamic defers member/type checking to runtime.
questions.detailedAnswer: var is compile-time type inference; object is the base type and may require casting; dynamic defers member/type checking to runtime.
questions.example: A strongly typed ATM response DTO should normally use var or an explicit type, not dynamic.
questions.seniorPerspective: Prefer compile-time safety. Use dynamic only when a genuine runtime shape requires it.
questions.memoryCue: var is still strongly typed; dynamic is runtime-bound.

questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP?
questions.shortAnswer: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Together they help model behaviour while controlling dependencies and change.
questions.detailedAnswer: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Together they help model behaviour while controlling dependencies and change.
questions.example: An ATM withdrawal service can hide validation details behind a method while different account types provide different withdrawal rules.
questions.seniorPerspective: For a senior answer, explain why composition and interfaces are often preferred over deep inheritance trees.
questions.memoryCue: Hide details, expose behaviour, reuse safely, substitute implementations.

questions.question: How would you explain SOLID with a real backend example?
questions.shortAnswer: SOLID is a set of design principles for reducing coupling and making change safer. In backend code, it often means small responsibilities, abstractions at change boundaries and dependencies flowing inward.
questions.detailedAnswer: SOLID is a set of design principles for reducing coupling and making change safer. In backend code, it often means small responsibilities, abstractions at change boundaries and dependencies flowing inward.
questions.example: An ATM transaction service should not validate cards, write audit logs, call the host and format UI messages in one class.
questions.seniorPerspective: Do not present SOLID as five definitions only; explain the coupling problem each principle prevents.
questions.memoryCue: SOLID = make change local and dependencies replaceable.

questions.question: When would you use List, HashSet and Dictionary?
questions.shortAnswer: List is ordered and indexable, HashSet stores unique values efficiently, and Dictionary maps keys to values.
questions.detailedAnswer: List is ordered and indexable, HashSet stores unique values efficiently, and Dictionary maps keys to values.
questions.example: Use a List for transaction history, a HashSet for already-processed transaction IDs and a Dictionary for terminal configuration by terminal ID.
questions.seniorPerspective: Choose based on required operations and expected scale, not habit.
questions.memoryCue: List = sequence; HashSet = uniqueness; Dictionary = lookup.

questions.question: Why use generics in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Generics provide type safety and reusable algorithms without forcing callers to cast or unnecessarily box value types.
questions.detailedAnswer: Generics provide type safety and reusable algorithms without forcing callers to cast or unnecessarily box value types.
questions.example: A generic repository or result type can work with Customer, Transaction and Account types while preserving compile-time safety.
questions.seniorPerspective: Mention generic constraints when the algorithm needs capabilities from T.
questions.memoryCue: Generics = reusable code + compile-time type safety.

questions.question: What is a delegate in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. It allows a method to be passed as a parameter or stored and invoked later.
questions.detailedAnswer: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. It allows a method to be passed as a parameter or stored and invoked later.
questions.example: A validation service can accept a delegate representing a rule that must pass before processing a transaction.
questions.seniorPerspective: Know the relationship between delegates, lambdas, Func, Action and events.
questions.memoryCue: Delegate = type-safe method reference.
questions.codeExample:
Func<decimal, bool> limitCheck = amount => amount <= 10000;
bool allowed = limitCheck(5000);

questions.question: What is the difference between a delegate and an event?
questions.shortAnswer: A delegate can be invoked by code that has access to it; an event restricts invocation so only the declaring type can raise it while subscribers can attach and detach.
questions.detailedAnswer: A delegate can be invoked by code that has access to it; an event restricts invocation so only the declaring type can raise it while subscribers can attach and detach.
questions.example: A transaction service can expose TransactionCompleted as an event; callers subscribe but cannot directly raise the event.
questions.seniorPerspective: Use events for notification, not as a general-purpose service communication mechanism.
questions.memoryCue: Event = controlled publisher; subscribers listen.

questions.question: What is the purpose of try, catch and finally?
questions.shortAnswer: try contains risky code, catch handles an exception and finally performs cleanup that should happen regardless of success or failure.
questions.detailedAnswer: try contains risky code, catch handles an exception and finally performs cleanup that should happen regardless of success or failure.
questions.example: A database connection or stream may need cleanup even when a transaction fails.
questions.seniorPerspective: Catch exceptions you can actually handle; do not use exceptions for ordinary control flow.
questions.memoryCue: catch handles; finally cleans up.

questions.question: Why should you use throw instead of throw ex when rethrowing?
questions.shortAnswer: throw preserves the original stack trace, while throw ex resets the stack trace to the rethrow location.
questions.detailedAnswer: throw preserves the original stack trace, while throw ex resets the stack trace to the rethrow location.
questions.example: A production ATM failure needs the original call path so the RCA points to the actual source of failure.
questions.seniorPerspective: At senior level, discuss exception boundaries, structured logging and translating infrastructure exceptions into domain/API errors.
questions.memoryCue: throw = preserve the original evidence.

questions.question: What is deferred execution in LINQ?
questions.shortAnswer: A LINQ query is often not executed when it is defined; it executes when enumerated or materialized.
questions.detailedAnswer: A LINQ query is often not executed when it is defined; it executes when enumerated or materialized.
questions.example: An EF Core query can be composed with filters first and sent to SQL only when ToListAsync is called.
questions.seniorPerspective: Be careful with repeated enumeration because it can repeat database work.
questions.memoryCue: Build first; execute on enumeration/materialization.
questions.codeExample:
var query = db.Transactions.Where(x => x.Amount > 1000);
var results = await query.ToListAsync();

questions.question: What is the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?
questions.shortAnswer: IEnumerable represents in-process enumeration, while IQueryable builds an expression tree that a provider such as EF Core can translate to a data source query.
questions.detailedAnswer: IEnumerable represents in-process enumeration, while IQueryable builds an expression tree that a provider such as EF Core can translate to a data source query.
questions.example: Filtering IQueryable before ToList lets SQL perform the filtering instead of loading rows and filtering in memory.
questions.seniorPerspective: A senior answer should mention generated SQL, translation limitations and premature materialization.
questions.memoryCue: IQueryable can push work to the provider; IEnumerable runs in memory.

questions.question: Does async/await create a new thread?
questions.shortAnswer: No. For I/O-bound work, async/await allows the current thread to return to the pool while the I/O completes; continuation resumes later.
questions.detailedAnswer: No. For I/O-bound work, async/await allows the current thread to return to the pool while the I/O completes; continuation resumes later.
questions.example: An API waiting for a database response should not block a thread with .Result or .Wait().
questions.seniorPerspective: Separate I/O concurrency from CPU parallelism when explaining async.
questions.memoryCue: Async I/O frees the thread; it is not automatic parallelism.

questions.question: How would you prevent thread-pool starvation in an ASP.NET Core API?
questions.shortAnswer: Avoid synchronous blocking, use async I/O end-to-end, bound expensive work, and investigate long-running CPU or blocking operations with runtime metrics and traces.
questions.detailedAnswer: Avoid synchronous blocking, use async I/O end-to-end, bound expensive work, and investigate long-running CPU or blocking operations with runtime metrics and traces.
questions.example: If many requests call .Result on database tasks, worker threads can become blocked and throughput collapses under load.
questions.seniorPerspective: At senior level, mention cancellation, bounded concurrency and measuring before changing ThreadPool settings.
questions.memoryCue: Never block a worker waiting for I/O.

questions.question: How does garbage collection work in .NET?
questions.shortAnswer: The GC automatically reclaims unreachable managed objects. It uses generations so short-lived objects can be collected efficiently without scanning the entire managed heap every time.
questions.detailedAnswer: The GC automatically reclaims unreachable managed objects. It uses generations so short-lived objects can be collected efficiently without scanning the entire managed heap every time.
questions.example: A request creates temporary DTOs and strings; most die young and are handled by Gen 0 collections.
questions.seniorPerspective: Know Gen 0/1/2, allocation pressure and why IDisposable is separate.
questions.memoryCue: GC manages managed memory; it does not replace deterministic resource cleanup.
questions.codeExample:
var dto = new TransactionDto();
// When unreachable, the GC can reclaim it.

questions.question: Why is IDisposable needed if .NET has garbage collection?
questions.shortAnswer: GC reclaims managed memory, but resources such as file handles, sockets and database connections need deterministic release.
questions.detailedAnswer: GC reclaims managed memory, but resources such as file handles, sockets and database connections need deterministic release.
questions.example: A DbConnection should be disposed promptly rather than waiting for GC.
questions.seniorPerspective: At senior level, distinguish memory leaks from resource leaks and explain using/await using.
questions.memoryCue: GC memory; Dispose resources.
questions.codeExample:
await using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
await connection.OpenAsync();

questions.question: What are CLR, JIT and managed code?
questions.shortAnswer: The CLR provides the execution environment, including GC and type/runtime services. JIT compiles IL into native machine code when needed. Managed code runs under these runtime services.
questions.detailedAnswer: The CLR provides the execution environment, including GC and type/runtime services. JIT compiles IL into native machine code when needed. Managed code runs under these runtime services.
questions.example: A C# API compiles to IL and the runtime executes it on the target machine.
questions.seniorPerspective: Avoid saying the CLR is simply the compiler; compilation and runtime execution are different stages.
questions.memoryCue: C# becomes IL; CLR executes it; JIT produces native code.
questions.codeExample:
public int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;
// C# -> IL -> JIT/native execution

questions.question: What is the difference between JIT and Native AOT?
questions.shortAnswer: JIT compiles code at runtime, while Native AOT compiles ahead of time to native code. AOT can improve startup and footprint but restricts scenarios relying on runtime code generation/reflection.
questions.detailedAnswer: JIT compiles code at runtime, while Native AOT compiles ahead of time to native code. AOT can improve startup and footprint but restricts scenarios relying on runtime code generation/reflection.
questions.example: A short-lived API or serverless workload may benefit from faster startup if its dependency graph is AOT-compatible.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior reasoning is about startup, memory, compatibility, reflection and deployment trade-offs, not declaring one universally better.
questions.memoryCue: JIT = runtime compilation; AOT = build-time native compilation.
questions.codeExample:
// Standard deployment: runtime JITs methods as needed.
// Native AOT: compile the application ahead of time.

questions.question: What are Transient, Scoped and Singleton lifetimes?
questions.shortAnswer: Transient creates a new instance per resolution, Scoped normally creates one per request scope, and Singleton creates one for the application lifetime.
questions.detailedAnswer: Transient creates a new instance per resolution, Scoped normally creates one per request scope, and Singleton creates one for the application lifetime.
questions.example: DbContext is commonly scoped, while a stateless configuration/cache service may be singleton.
questions.seniorPerspective: A singleton must be thread-safe and must not capture a scoped dependency.
questions.memoryCue: Transient = resolution; Scoped = request; Singleton = application.

questions.question: What is a captive dependency in .NET DI?
questions.shortAnswer: A captive dependency occurs when a longer-lived service holds a shorter-lived dependency, such as a singleton holding a scoped service.
questions.detailedAnswer: A captive dependency occurs when a longer-lived service holds a shorter-lived dependency, such as a singleton holding a scoped service.
questions.example: A singleton that captures a request-scoped DbContext can cause incorrect state sharing and lifetime problems.
questions.seniorPerspective: Know how to create a scope explicitly for background work instead of injecting scoped services into singleton workers.
questions.memoryCue: Long-lived object must not capture shorter-lived state.

questions.question: How does configuration work in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: ASP.NET Core builds configuration from providers such as JSON files, environment variables, command-line arguments and secret stores, with later providers able to override earlier values.
questions.detailedAnswer: ASP.NET Core builds configuration from providers such as JSON files, environment variables, command-line arguments and secret stores, with later providers able to override earlier values.
questions.example: A database connection setting can come from appsettings locally and an environment/secret provider in production.
questions.seniorPerspective: Do not put production secrets directly into source-controlled appsettings files.
questions.memoryCue: Configuration is layered; environment-specific values can override defaults.
questions.codeExample: var value = builder.Configuration["Database:ConnectionString"];

questions.question: What is the Options pattern?
questions.shortAnswer: The Options pattern binds a configuration section to a strongly typed class, making configuration easier to validate and inject.
questions.detailedAnswer: The Options pattern binds a configuration section to a strongly typed class, making configuration easier to validate and inject.
questions.example: An ATM host endpoint and timeout can be represented by a typed HostOptions object.
questions.seniorPerspective: For senior interviews, mention validation and the difference between IOptions, IOptionsSnapshot and IOptionsMonitor.
questions.memoryCue: Options = strongly typed configuration.

questions.question: Why is structured logging better than string-only logging?
questions.shortAnswer: Structured logging records named properties separately from the message, making logs easier to search, aggregate and correlate.
questions.detailedAnswer: Structured logging records named properties separately from the message, making logs easier to search, aggregate and correlate.
questions.example: Instead of embedding a terminal ID in a string, log it as a property so production support can filter all events for that terminal.
questions.seniorPerspective: Choose stable business/technical dimensions and avoid secrets, PINs, tokens or sensitive customer data.
questions.memoryCue: Log properties, not just sentences.
questions.codeExample: logger.LogInformation("Withdrawal completed {TerminalId} {Amount}", terminalId, amount);

questions.question: What should you log when diagnosing a production API failure?
questions.shortAnswer: Log the operation, correlation/trace identifier, relevant non-sensitive identifiers, dependency outcome, timing and exception details while avoiding secrets and excessive payloads.
questions.detailedAnswer: Log the operation, correlation/trace identifier, relevant non-sensitive identifiers, dependency outcome, timing and exception details while avoiding secrets and excessive payloads.
questions.example: For an ATM transaction failure, a correlation ID plus terminal ID, operation and downstream latency can connect API logs with host logs.
questions.seniorPerspective: Logging is part of observability; pair logs with metrics and traces.
questions.memoryCue: Logs should answer what, where, when and which request.

questions.question: What happens when an HTTP request enters an ASP.NET Core application?
questions.shortAnswer: The request travels through the middleware pipeline, routing selects an endpoint, model binding/validation and endpoint logic run, and the response travels back through middleware.
questions.detailedAnswer: The request travels through the middleware pipeline, routing selects an endpoint, model binding/validation and endpoint logic run, and the response travels back through middleware.
questions.example: An ATM management API request can pass through exception handling, authentication, routing and the controller endpoint.
questions.seniorPerspective: Middleware order is part of correctness, especially for security and exception handling.
questions.memoryCue: Request enters pipeline; middleware wraps endpoint execution.

questions.question: What is model binding and validation in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Model binding maps route, query, header and body data to .NET parameters/models. Validation checks whether the resulting model satisfies defined rules.
questions.detailedAnswer: Model binding maps route, query, header and body data to .NET parameters/models. Validation checks whether the resulting model satisfies defined rules.
questions.example: A withdrawal request can require a positive amount and a valid account identifier before service logic executes.
questions.seniorPerspective: Keep validation close to the API contract but keep business rules in the domain/service layer.
questions.memoryCue: Binding builds the object; validation checks it.

questions.question: What makes a good ASP.NET Core Web API endpoint?
questions.shortAnswer: It has a clear resource/operation contract, correct HTTP semantics, validation, consistent errors, cancellation and appropriate status codes.
questions.detailedAnswer: It has a clear resource/operation contract, correct HTTP semantics, validation, consistent errors, cancellation and appropriate status codes.
questions.example: POST /transactions can create a transaction and return 201 with a resource/location when creation succeeds.
questions.seniorPerspective: Keep controllers thin and put business orchestration in services/use cases.
questions.memoryCue: API contract = semantics + validation + consistent errors.

questions.question: How would you design consistent API error responses?
questions.shortAnswer: Use a stable error contract containing a status, machine-readable code, human-readable detail and correlation information, while avoiding internal stack traces.
questions.detailedAnswer: Use a stable error contract containing a status, machine-readable code, human-readable detail and correlation information, while avoiding internal stack traces.
questions.example: A downstream timeout can become a controlled 503 response with an error code the Angular client can handle.
questions.seniorPerspective: Consistency matters for clients, monitoring and support. Use global exception handling rather than repeating try/catch in every controller.
questions.memoryCue: Stable error contract; never leak internals.

questions.question: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Middleware is a component in the HTTP pipeline that can inspect, modify, short-circuit or pass a request to the next component.
questions.detailedAnswer: Middleware is a component in the HTTP pipeline that can inspect, modify, short-circuit or pass a request to the next component.
questions.example: A correlation-ID middleware can read or create an ID and attach it to logs before calling the next middleware.
questions.seniorPerspective: A middleware can run code before and after next(), which is useful for timing and response processing.
questions.memoryCue: Middleware wraps the request pipeline.

questions.question: Why does middleware order matter?
questions.shortAnswer: Middleware executes in registration order on the request path and in reverse order on the response path; earlier middleware can also short-circuit later components.
questions.detailedAnswer: Middleware executes in registration order on the request path and in reverse order on the response path; earlier middleware can also short-circuit later components.
questions.example: Authentication must occur before authorization so the authorization layer has an authenticated principal.
questions.seniorPerspective: Explain ordering using the dependency between components rather than memorising one fixed template.
questions.memoryCue: Pipeline order changes behaviour.

questions.question: What are filters in ASP.NET Core MVC?
questions.shortAnswer: Filters run at defined stages around MVC/controller execution, such as authorization, action execution, exception handling and result processing.
questions.detailedAnswer: Filters run at defined stages around MVC/controller execution, such as authorization, action execution, exception handling and result processing.
questions.example: An action filter can measure execution time for selected controllers without putting timing code inside every action.
questions.seniorPerspective: Choose filters for MVC-specific cross-cutting behaviour and middleware for request-pipeline concerns.
questions.memoryCue: Filters target MVC/action stages; middleware targets the broader HTTP pipeline.

questions.question: When would you choose middleware versus an action filter?
questions.shortAnswer: Use middleware for concerns independent of MVC such as correlation IDs or global exception handling; use filters when the concern depends on controller/action metadata or MVC execution.
questions.detailedAnswer: Use middleware for concerns independent of MVC such as correlation IDs or global exception handling; use filters when the concern depends on controller/action metadata or MVC execution.
questions.example: Authorization-like behaviour that needs action metadata may belong at the filter/policy layer, while request timing for every endpoint can be middleware.
questions.seniorPerspective: Make the choice based on scope and available context, not preference.
questions.memoryCue: Middleware = HTTP pipeline; filter = MVC pipeline.

questions.question: What are the main HTTP methods and their typical semantics?
questions.shortAnswer: GET retrieves, POST creates or triggers a non-idempotent operation, PUT replaces a resource, PATCH partially updates it and DELETE removes it. Semantics matter for clients, caching and retries.
questions.detailedAnswer: GET retrieves, POST creates or triggers a non-idempotent operation, PUT replaces a resource, PATCH partially updates it and DELETE removes it. Semantics matter for clients, caching and retries.
questions.example: GET /accounts/123 retrieves an account; PATCH /accounts/123 changes selected fields.
questions.seniorPerspective: Be precise about idempotency: PUT and DELETE are intended to be idempotent; POST generally is not.
questions.memoryCue: GET read; POST create/action; PUT replace; PATCH partial; DELETE remove.

questions.question: What does idempotency mean in an API?
questions.shortAnswer: An idempotent operation can be repeated with the same intended effect as executing it once. It is critical when clients retry after timeouts.
questions.detailedAnswer: An idempotent operation can be repeated with the same intended effect as executing it once. It is critical when clients retry after timeouts.
questions.example: A withdrawal request must not dispense cash twice if the client retries because the first response was lost; use an idempotency key and server-side state.
questions.seniorPerspective: For money movement, discuss atomic persistence, uniqueness constraints and what happens if the downstream side effect occurs before the key is recorded.
questions.memoryCue: Idempotency protects retries from duplicate effects.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.shortAnswer: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization determines what that authenticated identity is allowed to do.
questions.detailedAnswer: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization determines what that authenticated identity is allowed to do.
questions.example: A user can authenticate successfully but still be unauthorized to approve a high-value transaction.
questions.seniorPerspective: Mention claims, roles and policies, and keep authorization decisions server-side.
questions.memoryCue: Authentication = who; authorization = what they can do.

questions.question: How does JWT bearer authentication work in an ASP.NET Core API?
questions.shortAnswer: The client sends a signed JWT access token. The API validates signature, issuer, audience and lifetime, then builds a ClaimsPrincipal used by authorization policies.
questions.detailedAnswer: The client sends a signed JWT access token. The API validates signature, issuer, audience and lifetime, then builds a ClaimsPrincipal used by authorization policies.
questions.example: An Angular client sends Authorization: Bearer <token> when calling the backend.
questions.seniorPerspective: Do not treat possession of a JWT as authorization for every endpoint; validate token parameters and least-privilege scopes/claims.
questions.memoryCue: JWT proves an issued identity/token; policies decide access.

questions.question: How do you prevent SQL injection in .NET?
questions.shortAnswer: Use parameterized queries or ORM APIs that parameterize values; never concatenate untrusted input into SQL.
questions.detailedAnswer: Use parameterized queries or ORM APIs that parameterize values; never concatenate untrusted input into SQL.
questions.example: An account number supplied by an API caller must be treated as data, not SQL syntax.
questions.seniorPerspective: Also validate input and restrict database permissions; parameterization is not a replacement for authorization.
questions.memoryCue: Parameters, not string concatenation.

questions.question: What security controls should a production ASP.NET Core API have?
questions.shortAnswer: At minimum: strong authentication, authorization policies, input validation, secure headers, HTTPS, secret management, dependency scanning, safe error handling, rate limiting where appropriate and audit/observability controls.
questions.detailedAnswer: At minimum: strong authentication, authorization policies, input validation, secure headers, HTTPS, secret management, dependency scanning, safe error handling, rate limiting where appropriate and audit/observability controls.
questions.example: A transaction API should enforce permissions, validate amounts, avoid sensitive logging and protect endpoints from abuse.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior answers connect controls to threats and explain how they are tested and monitored.
questions.memoryCue: Security is layered; no single control is enough.

questions.question: What is DbContext and why is its lifetime usually scoped?
questions.shortAnswer: DbContext represents a unit of work for querying and saving entities. A scoped lifetime commonly maps one context to one web request.
questions.detailedAnswer: DbContext represents a unit of work for querying and saving entities. A scoped lifetime commonly maps one context to one web request.
questions.example: A withdrawal request can load an account, update its state and save the transaction using one request-scoped context.
questions.seniorPerspective: DbContext is not thread-safe; do not run parallel operations on one instance.
questions.memoryCue: DbContext = unit of work + change tracking.
questions.codeExample:
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(options =>
    options.UseSqlServer(connectionString));

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem in EF Core?
questions.shortAnswer: N+1 occurs when one query loads parent rows and then an additional query runs for each parent, producing many round trips.
questions.detailedAnswer: N+1 occurs when one query loads parent rows and then an additional query runs for each parent, producing many round trips.
questions.example: Loading 100 accounts and querying transactions separately for each can result in 101 database calls.
questions.seniorPerspective: Use projection, Include when appropriate, batching and SQL/query inspection; do not blindly add Include everywhere.
questions.memoryCue: One logical request should not accidentally become N+1 database calls.

questions.question: What is a database index and why does it help?
questions.shortAnswer: An index is a data structure that helps the database locate rows efficiently, reducing work for suitable predicates and orderings.
questions.detailedAnswer: An index is a data structure that helps the database locate rows efficiently, reducing work for suitable predicates and orderings.
questions.example: If transaction lookups frequently use TerminalId and CreatedAt, an appropriate composite index can avoid scanning the entire table.
questions.seniorPerspective: Indexes must match access patterns; too many indexes increase write cost and storage.
questions.memoryCue: Index = faster reads at storage/write cost.
questions.codeExample:
CREATE INDEX IX_Transactions_TerminalId_CreatedAt
ON Transactions(TerminalId, CreatedAt);

questions.question: What are transaction isolation levels and why do they matter?
questions.shortAnswer: Isolation levels control how concurrent transactions can observe each other's changes, balancing consistency, locking and concurrency.
questions.detailedAnswer: Isolation levels control how concurrent transactions can observe each other's changes, balancing consistency, locking and concurrency.
questions.example: Two ATM operations updating the same account need a concurrency strategy so a balance cannot be incorrectly overwritten.
questions.seniorPerspective: Discuss lost updates, dirty/non-repeatable/phantom reads and the database-specific implementation.
questions.memoryCue: Isolation controls concurrent visibility and anomalies.

questions.question: Why should business logic not live inside controllers?
questions.shortAnswer: Controllers should coordinate HTTP concerns; business rules belong in domain/application services where they can be tested and reused independently of HTTP.
questions.detailedAnswer: Controllers should coordinate HTTP concerns; business rules belong in domain/application services where they can be tested and reused independently of HTTP.
questions.example: Withdrawal limits should not be embedded in an HTTP action because another channel may also initiate the transaction.
questions.seniorPerspective: Use architecture to make dependencies and change boundaries explicit, not just to create more projects.
questions.memoryCue: Controller = transport boundary; service/domain = business behaviour.

questions.question: What is the Strategy pattern and where could it help in a backend?
questions.shortAnswer: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface, allowing selection without a large conditional block.
questions.detailedAnswer: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface, allowing selection without a large conditional block.
questions.example: Different ATM transaction types or fee calculation rules can use different strategies.
questions.seniorPerspective: Choose a pattern when it reduces a real design problem; do not force patterns into simple code.
questions.memoryCue: Strategy = interchangeable behaviour.

questions.question: Why use caching in a backend?
questions.shortAnswer: Caching avoids repeated expensive work or I/O by storing reusable results closer to the application or client.
questions.detailedAnswer: Caching avoids repeated expensive work or I/O by storing reusable results closer to the application or client.
questions.example: ATM configuration metadata that changes rarely can be cached instead of loaded from the database on every request.
questions.seniorPerspective: Every cached value needs an invalidation/expiry strategy.
questions.memoryCue: Cache = trade memory for lower latency/load.

questions.question: What problems can distributed caching introduce?
questions.shortAnswer: It introduces consistency, serialization, network latency, expiration, stampede and availability concerns because the cache is now a distributed dependency.
questions.detailedAnswer: It introduces consistency, serialization, network latency, expiration, stampede and availability concerns because the cache is now a distributed dependency.
questions.example: Several API instances may read the same terminal configuration from Redis; an update must invalidate or version the cached value correctly.
questions.seniorPerspective: Discuss TTL, invalidation, cache-aside, stampede protection and what happens when Redis is unavailable.
questions.memoryCue: Distributed cache improves sharing but adds distributed-system failure modes.
questions.codeExample:
var key = $"terminal:{terminalId}:v{version}";
await distributedCache.SetStringAsync(key, json);

questions.question: How do you approach a slow ASP.NET Core API?
questions.shortAnswer: Measure first: identify whether time is spent in application CPU, database, network, serialization or external dependencies. Then optimize the dominant bottleneck and verify with realistic tests.
questions.detailedAnswer: Measure first: identify whether time is spent in application CPU, database, network, serialization or external dependencies. Then optimize the dominant bottleneck and verify with realistic tests.
questions.example: If an endpoint is slow, inspect traces and SQL timings before changing code randomly.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior performance work is evidence-driven; avoid premature micro-optimizations.
questions.memoryCue: Measure → find bottleneck → change → verify.

questions.question: How would you scale a high-throughput .NET API?
questions.shortAnswer: Keep application instances stateless, use async I/O, optimize database access, add appropriate caching, scale horizontally and protect dependencies with timeouts, bounded concurrency and backpressure.
questions.detailedAnswer: Keep application instances stateless, use async I/O, optimize database access, add appropriate caching, scale horizontally and protect dependencies with timeouts, bounded concurrency and backpressure.
questions.example: An ATM configuration API can run multiple instances behind a load balancer while shared state lives in appropriate data stores.
questions.seniorPerspective: Discuss database capacity, connection pools, cache hit rate, latency percentiles and failure behaviour—not just adding more servers.
questions.memoryCue: Scale out statelessly; protect bottlenecks.

questions.question: What is boxing and unboxing in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Boxing converts a value type to object or an implemented interface, allocating an object; unboxing extracts the value type back. Repeated boxing can create unnecessary allocations.
questions.detailedAnswer: Boxing converts a value type to object or an implemented interface, allocating an object; unboxing extracts the value type back. Repeated boxing can create unnecessary allocations.
questions.example: A generic collection avoids boxing that older non-generic collections could cause when storing transaction counters.
questions.seniorPerspective: Avoid boxing in hot paths; generics usually provide better type safety and allocation behaviour.
questions.memoryCue: Boxing = value becomes object; unboxing = object becomes value.

questions.question: What is the difference between abstraction and encapsulation?
questions.shortAnswer: Abstraction exposes what a component does while hiding unnecessary implementation detail; encapsulation controls access to state and behaviour inside a type.
questions.detailedAnswer: Abstraction exposes what a component does while hiding unnecessary implementation detail; encapsulation controls access to state and behaviour inside a type.
questions.example: A withdrawal service exposes WithdrawAsync while keeping validation and state-transition details internal.
questions.seniorPerspective: Good design uses both: a stable abstraction at the boundary and encapsulated invariants inside the implementation.
questions.memoryCue: Abstraction = what; encapsulation = protect how/state.

questions.question: What is the difference between IEnumerable, ICollection and IList?
questions.shortAnswer: IEnumerable provides enumeration, ICollection adds collection operations such as Count and mutation, while IList adds indexed access and insertion/removal by index.
questions.detailedAnswer: IEnumerable provides enumeration, ICollection adds collection operations such as Count and mutation, while IList adds indexed access and insertion/removal by index.
questions.example: A read-only service contract may expose IEnumerable<Transaction>; code needing indexed operations may use IList.
questions.seniorPerspective: Expose the least powerful abstraction the consumer needs.
questions.memoryCue: IEnumerable = enumerate; ICollection = collection operations; IList = indexed list.
questions.codeExample:
IEnumerable<Transaction> transactions = GetTransactions();
foreach(var t in transactions) Console.WriteLine(t.Id);

questions.question: What is the difference between Action, Func and Predicate?
questions.shortAnswer: Action represents a method returning void, Func represents a method returning a value, and Predicate is a delegate returning bool for a condition.
questions.detailedAnswer: Action represents a method returning void, Func represents a method returning a value, and Predicate is a delegate returning bool for a condition.
questions.example: Validation rules commonly fit Predicate or Func<bool>-style delegates.
questions.seniorPerspective: Know the generic parameter ordering and use named delegates when the business meaning deserves a domain-specific type.
questions.memoryCue: Action = void; Func = value; Predicate = bool condition.

questions.question: What is the difference between throwing exceptions and returning error results?
questions.shortAnswer: Exceptions are appropriate for exceptional failures and cross-layer propagation; expected business outcomes can often be represented explicitly as a result type.
questions.detailedAnswer: Exceptions are appropriate for exceptional failures and cross-layer propagation; expected business outcomes can often be represented explicitly as a result type.
questions.example: Insufficient funds is a predictable business outcome, while a database connection failure is an exceptional infrastructure failure.
questions.seniorPerspective: Avoid both extremes: do not throw for every validation failure, and do not hide infrastructure failures in arbitrary result strings.
questions.memoryCue: Expected outcome = result; exceptional failure = exception.

questions.question: What is the difference between Select and SelectMany?
questions.shortAnswer: Select transforms each source element into one result, while SelectMany transforms each element into a sequence and flattens the nested sequences.
questions.detailedAnswer: Select transforms each source element into one result, while SelectMany transforms each element into a sequence and flattens the nested sequences.
questions.example: An account has many transactions; SelectMany can produce one flat sequence of transactions across accounts.
questions.seniorPerspective: Use SelectMany carefully with large datasets and ensure EF Core can translate the resulting query.
questions.memoryCue: Select = map; SelectMany = map + flatten.
questions.codeExample: var allTransactions = accounts.SelectMany(a => a.Transactions);

questions.question: When should you use Task.WhenAll?
questions.shortAnswer: Use Task.WhenAll when independent asynchronous operations can safely run concurrently and you want to await their combined completion.
questions.detailedAnswer: Use Task.WhenAll when independent asynchronous operations can safely run concurrently and you want to await their combined completion.
questions.example: Loading terminal configuration and feature flags independently can be concurrent if neither operation depends on the other.
questions.seniorPerspective: Do not use uncontrolled concurrency against a database or downstream service; bound concurrency when load is large.
questions.memoryCue: Independent I/O → WhenAll.

questions.question: What causes unnecessary allocations in a .NET API?
questions.shortAnswer: Creating excessive temporary objects, strings, arrays, closures or boxed values can increase allocation rate and GC pressure.
questions.detailedAnswer: Creating excessive temporary objects, strings, arrays, closures or boxed values can increase allocation rate and GC pressure.
questions.example: Building many intermediate strings for every transaction response can create avoidable allocations.
questions.seniorPerspective: Measure allocations with profiling before optimizing; readability usually matters more until a real hotspot is proven.
questions.memoryCue: Allocation rate matters under load.
questions.codeExample: var message = $"Transaction {id} completed";

questions.question: What is an assembly in .NET?
questions.shortAnswer: An assembly is a compiled deployment/versioning unit containing IL, metadata and related resources, typically represented by a DLL or executable.
questions.detailedAnswer: An assembly is a compiled deployment/versioning unit containing IL, metadata and related resources, typically represented by a DLL or executable.
questions.example: A backend service references application and library assemblies when it starts.
questions.seniorPerspective: Know the difference between source project, assembly, namespace and type; they are not interchangeable concepts.
questions.memoryCue: Assembly = compiled unit + metadata.
questions.codeExample: // MyService.dll is an assembly containing compiled types and metadata.

questions.question: Why is constructor injection preferred in .NET?
questions.shortAnswer: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit, ensures the object cannot normally exist without them and improves testability.
questions.detailedAnswer: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit, ensures the object cannot normally exist without them and improves testability.
questions.example: A transaction service can declare its repository and audit writer in its constructor instead of resolving them from a service locator.
questions.seniorPerspective: Avoid injecting IServiceProvider everywhere; it hides dependencies and often becomes a service-locator anti-pattern.
questions.memoryCue: Required dependencies belong in the constructor.

questions.question: How should configuration differ between development and production?
questions.shortAnswer: Keep safe defaults in source-controlled configuration and supply environment-specific values through deployment configuration or secret providers. Never depend on developer-machine settings in production.
questions.detailedAnswer: Keep safe defaults in source-controlled configuration and supply environment-specific values through deployment configuration or secret providers. Never depend on developer-machine settings in production.
questions.example: A local SQL connection string can be in development settings, while production receives its value from a secure deployment mechanism.
questions.seniorPerspective: Configuration should be validated at startup when invalid settings would make the service unusable.
questions.memoryCue: Code stays the same; environment supplies values.
questions.codeExample: var connection = builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default");

questions.question: What is the purpose of log levels such as Information, Warning and Error?
questions.shortAnswer: Log levels communicate severity and operational importance. Information describes normal significant operations, Warning indicates something unexpected but handled, and Error indicates a failed operation.
questions.detailedAnswer: Log levels communicate severity and operational importance. Information describes normal significant operations, Warning indicates something unexpected but handled, and Error indicates a failed operation.
questions.example: A retryable downstream timeout may be Warning if handled; a failed transaction may be Error.
questions.seniorPerspective: Choose levels so production teams can filter noise without losing evidence.
questions.memoryCue: Level = operational severity.

questions.question: What is dependency injection in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: ASP.NET Core has a built-in DI container where services are registered and resolved, usually through constructor injection.
questions.detailedAnswer: ASP.NET Core has a built-in DI container where services are registered and resolved, usually through constructor injection.
questions.example: A controller receives ITransactionService without constructing the concrete implementation itself.
questions.seniorPerspective: DI is primarily about dependency management and composition; it is not automatically a design architecture.
questions.memoryCue: Register abstraction → inject abstraction.
questions.codeExample: builder.Services.AddScoped<ITransactionService, TransactionService>();

questions.question: Which HTTP status codes should a backend developer know well?
questions.shortAnswer: Common codes include 200 for success, 201 for creation, 204 for successful no-content operations, 400 for invalid requests, 401 for unauthenticated access, 403 for forbidden access, 404 for missing resources and 500/503 for server/dependency failures.
questions.detailedAnswer: Common codes include 200 for success, 201 for creation, 204 for successful no-content operations, 400 for invalid requests, 401 for unauthenticated access, 403 for forbidden access, 404 for missing resources and 500/503 for server/dependency failures.
questions.example: A valid POST creating a transaction can return 201; an unauthenticated request should normally return 401.
questions.seniorPerspective: Be consistent across the API and do not return 200 for every error.
questions.memoryCue: Status code communicates outcome semantics.
questions.codeExample:
return CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get), new { id }, result);
// 404 when resource does not exist

questions.question: How do you write custom middleware?
questions.shortAnswer: A middleware receives HttpContext and a RequestDelegate, performs logic before and/or after calling the next delegate, and can short-circuit when needed.
questions.detailedAnswer: A middleware receives HttpContext and a RequestDelegate, performs logic before and/or after calling the next delegate, and can short-circuit when needed.
questions.example: Correlation IDs and request timing are common cross-cutting middleware concerns.
questions.seniorPerspective: Keep middleware focused; avoid putting business rules into the HTTP pipeline.
questions.memoryCue: Middleware wraps next().

questions.question: What is an authorization filter versus an action filter?
questions.shortAnswer: Authorization filters run early to determine access, while action filters wrap controller action execution and are useful for action-specific cross-cutting behaviour.
questions.detailedAnswer: Authorization filters run early to determine access, while action filters wrap controller action execution and are useful for action-specific cross-cutting behaviour.
questions.example: A timing filter can measure controller execution; authorization policies determine whether the caller may execute the endpoint.
questions.seniorPerspective: Prefer ASP.NET Core authorization policies for authorization rather than building custom access checks into arbitrary action filters.
questions.memoryCue: Authorization decides access; action filter wraps action execution.

questions.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
questions.shortAnswer: PUT generally replaces the resource representation and is intended to be idempotent; PATCH applies a partial modification and its semantics depend on the patch format.
questions.detailedAnswer: PUT generally replaces the resource representation and is intended to be idempotent; PATCH applies a partial modification and its semantics depend on the patch format.
questions.example: Updating an entire terminal configuration can use PUT; changing only one setting can use PATCH.
questions.seniorPerspective: Design APIs around resource semantics and document validation and idempotency behaviour.
questions.memoryCue: PUT = replace; PATCH = partial change.

questions.question: What are claims and policies in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Claims are pieces of information about an authenticated principal; policies combine requirements that determine whether a request is authorized.
questions.detailedAnswer: Claims are pieces of information about an authenticated principal; policies combine requirements that determine whether a request is authorized.
questions.example: A claim can identify a user's role or permission, while a policy can require the CanApprove permission.
questions.seniorPerspective: Policies are more flexible than scattering role checks through controllers.
questions.memoryCue: Claims describe identity; policies enforce access rules.
questions.codeExample:
builder.Services.AddAuthorization(o =>
    o.AddPolicy("CanApprove", p => p.RequireClaim("permission","approve")));

questions.question: What is the difference between hashing and encryption?
questions.shortAnswer: Hashing is designed as a one-way transformation, while encryption is reversible with a key. Passwords should use dedicated password hashing; sensitive data requiring recovery uses encryption.
questions.detailedAnswer: Hashing is designed as a one-way transformation, while encryption is reversible with a key. Passwords should use dedicated password hashing; sensitive data requiring recovery uses encryption.
questions.example: User passwords are verified using password hashes; a secret that must later be recovered may require encryption.
questions.seniorPerspective: Do not invent cryptography; use well-established framework/library primitives and key management.
questions.memoryCue: Hash = one-way verification; encryption = reversible protection.
questions.codeExample:
var hash = passwordHasher.HashPassword(user, password);
var result = passwordHasher.VerifyHashedPassword(user, hash, password);

questions.question: What is AsNoTracking and when should you use it?
questions.shortAnswer: AsNoTracking disables change tracking for a query, which is often appropriate for read-only results and can reduce tracking overhead.
questions.detailedAnswer: AsNoTracking disables change tracking for a query, which is often appropriate for read-only results and can reduce tracking overhead.
questions.example: A dashboard endpoint returning transaction summaries does not need EF to track every entity.
questions.seniorPerspective: Do not use it blindly when you need to modify tracked entities later.
questions.memoryCue: Read-only query → consider no tracking.
questions.codeExample:
var rows = await db.Transactions
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Select(x => new { x.Id, x.Amount })
    .ToListAsync();

questions.question: What is a deadlock in a database?
questions.shortAnswer: A deadlock occurs when transactions wait on resources held by each other, so neither can proceed. The database detects it and normally aborts one transaction.
questions.detailedAnswer: A deadlock occurs when transactions wait on resources held by each other, so neither can proceed. The database detects it and normally aborts one transaction.
questions.example: Two transaction paths updating Account then Transaction in opposite orders can deadlock.
questions.seniorPerspective: Consistent lock ordering, short transactions and retry strategies can reduce impact; inspect deadlock graphs when diagnosing.
questions.memoryCue: Deadlock = circular waiting.

questions.question: What is Clean Architecture trying to achieve?
questions.shortAnswer: It keeps business rules independent of infrastructure and delivery mechanisms, with dependencies pointing toward stable inner layers.
questions.detailedAnswer: It keeps business rules independent of infrastructure and delivery mechanisms, with dependencies pointing toward stable inner layers.
questions.example: The ATM transaction rules should not depend directly on SQL Server or ASP.NET controllers.
questions.seniorPerspective: The goal is dependency direction and change isolation, not creating four projects for every small application.
questions.memoryCue: Business rules inside; infrastructure outside.

questions.question: What is cache-aside caching?
questions.shortAnswer: The application first checks the cache; on a miss it loads from the source, stores the result with an expiry and returns it.
questions.detailedAnswer: The application first checks the cache; on a miss it loads from the source, stores the result with an expiry and returns it.
questions.example: Terminal configuration is read from Redis first and from SQL when absent.
questions.seniorPerspective: Define TTL and invalidation rules; stale data is a design decision, not an accident.
questions.memoryCue: Read cache → miss → source → populate.

questions.question: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
questions.shortAnswer: Latency is the time taken by an individual operation; throughput is how much work the system completes per unit time.
questions.detailedAnswer: Latency is the time taken by an individual operation; throughput is how much work the system completes per unit time.
questions.example: An API may have 100 ms average latency while processing thousands of requests per second if it scales horizontally.
questions.seniorPerspective: Use percentiles such as p95/p99 for latency and inspect capacity bottlenecks when throughput increases.
questions.memoryCue: Latency = time per request; throughput = work per time.
